articles.title: Texas politics inflamed by MAGA cowboys v Indians row
articles.summary: US News: The TOI correspondent from Washington: The photograph that Bo French chose to make a political argument about Indians and foreigners overrunning the U.
articles.body: The TOI correspondent from Washington: The photograph that Bo French chose to make a political argument about Indians and foreigners overrunning the University of Texas, Austin, may have been worth thousands of social media posts, but it failed the statistical smell test.French, the Republican nominee for the powerful Texas Railroad Commission, posted a photograph of Longhorn fans -- named after the famous local cattle breed -- celebrating UT Austin’s dramatic September 12 football victory over Ohio State. Because a section of the crowd appeared heavily brown -- itself surprising because cricket-mad Indians are no great fans of American football -- French presented it as visual evidence of a demographic desi takeover.“I heard UT graduation this year looked like this. I didn’t believe it. The problem is now obviously far worse than anyone imagined," he wrote. He later doubled down, saying the image showed how “Americans have been displaced by foreigners” and lamenting that Texas families could not get their children into UT because the university “prioritizes foreigners over Texans.”There was, however, a small problem with the argument: UT's enrollment figures do not remotely resemble the photograph. For 2025-26, UT Austin reported 55,000 students, of whom 80.5% were Texas residents. Another 10.2% came from elsewhere in the U.S. International students accounted for about 6,877 students, and of those, 1,660 were from India, roughly 2.4% of total university enrollment -- a substantial community, but hardly evidence of a foreign or Indian invasion.There is another important statistical trap in the “Indians/foreigners have taken over” canard: “Asian” or “Indian” or “brown” is not synonymous with “foreign.” A foreign-looking student in a football crowd could be an American citizen, a permanent resident, a Texas-born child of immigrants or an international student. Race or apparent ethnicity cannot establish immigration status. The photo says rather more about Texas's changing demographics than about foreigners taking over UT.Asian Americans now constitute about 6.7% of Texas's population, while the state's foreign-born population is 17.6%, according to Census Bureau data. The transformation is particularly visible in the technology and professional suburbs around Dallas-Fort Worth, Houston and Austin which have become a hotbed of anti-Indian rhetoric and activism.Indian community activists acknowledge none of this means immigration policy is beyond legitimate debate, nor that every criticism of the H-1B programme is xenophobic. They agree that critics raise genuine questions about outsourcing, wage competition, employer practices, visa dependence and whether the programme is being used as Congress intended. But there is a considerable difference between asking whether H-1B policy works properly and looking at a football crowd, guessing people's ethnicity and declaring that Indians are displacing Americans.The distinction matters because Indians have increasingly become a conspicuous target in America's immigration debate. The H-1B program is heavily concentrated among Indian nationals, particularly in technology and other skilled occupations. As the visa debate has intensified, legitimate arguments about the program have increasingly merged online with claims, accompanied by ugly racial slurs and stereotyping, that Indians -- "jeets" in MAGA argot -- are “invaders” and “job stealers.”A Center for the Study of Organized Hate analysis of 680 high-engagement anti-Indian posts on X between July 1 and September 7, 2025, found that they generated 281 million views. Nearly 70% involved narratives about Indians as “invaders” or “job thieves,” alongside calls for deportation. French's UT post fits into that pattern: foreign status inferred from appearance, and appearance presented as evidence of institutional capture.The response from Texas Republicans exposed another fault line within the GOP. Senator John Cornyn, a Republican and former co-chair of the Senate India Caucus, sharply rebuked French, asking whether Republicans would condemn “intolerance and racism” or allow it to become normalized.“This is how great political parties self-destruct,” he warned. French, rather than retreating, attacked Cornyn as an “America Last” globalist and accused institutions of being overrun by illegal aliens and foreign nationals.The exchanges illustrate a larger Republican dilemma.Texas Governor Greg Abbott, who has made two business trips to India, has simultaneously pursued tough state-level immigration measures while maintaining a political and economic environment attractive to technology, energy and internationally connected businesses. In response to the controversy, Abbott rejected French's interpretation of the photograph, saying it showed how Texans could unite, while reiterating his support for stringent immigration policies and restrictions involving H-1B visas at universities. MAGA hardliner response: A meme showing Abbott smooching a sari clad woman who says, “Thank you for catering to us.”French's history makes the episode more combustible. He has previously made inflammatory comments about Muslims and Jews, advocated sweeping deportations and used provocative language about immigrants and Native Americans. In March, he called for deporting 100 million people — a figure that would corral almost a third of the U.S population and would necessarily encompass millions of American citizens.The political question now is whether Texas Republicans will continue treating visible demographic change as evidence of displacement or distinguish between immigration policy, economic competition and the much older question of who gets to call himself or herself a Texan – or American for that matter. For now, a football photograph has exposed a much deeper argument over immigration, race, economic opportunity and the changing meaning of “American” — while the statistics sit rather conspicuously on the sidelines.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: In 1990, Tennessee siblings planted 240 acres of former fields and pastures with loblolly pine; 28 years later, their entire 852-acre family property passed to a land trust for conservation
articles.summary: US News: An 852-acre family estate in Maury County, Tennessee, has been placed under permanent conservation, nearly three decades after a brother and sister be.
articles.body: An 852-acre family estate in Maury County, Tennessee, has been placed under permanent conservation, nearly three decades after a brother and sister began turning hundreds of acres of former farmland back into forest. According to The Land Trust for Tennessee, the property, known as the Sugg Property, was transferred directly to the organisation after original landowners Mary Ann Sugg and her brother John died. Their unconditional gift means the large landscape of pine forests, native woodlands, and open pastures will remain protected from commercial development forever. For local conservationists, the transfer completes a family legacy that began in the middle of the 20th century, when the property was a working dairy farm, and eventually turned into an important natural area.From Working Dairy Farm to Conservation HavenAccording to information from The Land Trust for Tennessee, the property's story began in 1955, when Mary Ann and John Sugg's father purchased the land and started a dairy farm that operated for many years. The siblings grew up on the property and developed a strong connection to its rolling hills and natural areas of Middle Tennessee. As farming needs changed, the siblings looked for ways to protect the property's soil and water. In 1990, they made an important decision to place the land in the federal Conservation Reserve Program. The program was created to take environmentally sensitive and highly erodible land out of active farming. As part of the program, the Sugg family planted 240 acres of former farm fields and open pastures with loblolly pine trees. Over the following decades, the young trees grew into thick and healthy forests. According to the land trust, the forests helped reduce soil erosion, improve the local environment, and create new habitats for wildlife.Formalising a Commitment to Permanent ProtectionThe decision to reforest nearly a third of the property was only the first part of Mary Ann and John Sugg's long-term conservation plans. According to The Land Trust for Tennessee, the siblings wanted to protect the entire 852-acre property from future development and division. They began working with the organisation to create formal legal protections for the land. In 2001, they donated their first voluntary conservation easement to the land trust. The agreement limited non-agricultural and commercial development across a large part of the property. Six years later, in 2007, they expanded that protection by donating a second conservation easement.During her lifetime, Mary Ann Sugg explained why she believed the land trust was the right organisation to protect the property. "The Land Trust for Tennessee is the perfect choice for making a planned gift. Its land conservation work is all about permanence — making sure that Tennessee's beautiful farms, forests, hiking trails, parks, and other special places remain as they are forever," she stated. "I take comfort knowing that my planned gift will help preserve the unique beauty of Tennessee long after I am gone."Unconditional Bequest Secures the Property's FutureAccording to The Land Trust for Tennessee, after both siblings died, their entire estate was transferred to the organisation as a direct bequest in 2018, 28 years after the original loblolly pine planting. Unlike some land donations that include strict conditions or complicated local agreements, the Sugg Property was given to the organisation without conditions. This gave the land trust greater freedom to manage and protect the property based on its environmental needs. The transfer allowed the organisation to manage the property directly as a conservation site. It also helped ensure that the environmental improvements made by the Sugg family over nearly three decades could continue. To help protect the 240 acres of loblolly pine and the surrounding native forests, the land trust re-enrolled the relevant acreage in the Conservation Reserve Program. According to the organisation, the federal conservation contracts will remain active through 2031.Active Land Management and Prescribed BurnsManaging an 852-acre forest requires regular work to keep the land healthy and protect it from environmental threats. The Land Trust for Tennessee uses several modern forestry practices at the Sugg Property, including carefully planned prescribed burns. According to the land trust, these controlled fires are used in the northern parts of the property and serve several important purposes:Controlling invasive plants that can threaten native vegetation.Removing built-up leaves and other forest material, which can lower the risk of large and uncontrolled wildfires.Returning important nutrients to the soil and supporting healthy plant growth.Encouraging native plants, increasing biodiversity, and improving habitats for wildlife.Through these continuing management efforts, the land trust works to keep the mature loblolly pine forests planted in 1990 healthy and strong.A Lasting Environmental Legacy for Middle TennesseeThe permanent protection of the Sugg Property represents a major private conservation achievement in Maury County. According to The Land Trust for Tennessee, the property helps protect regional watersheds, forest areas, and air quality as development continues to expand across Middle Tennessee. By combining the federal Conservation Reserve Program, voluntary conservation easements, and the eventual donation of their entire property, Mary Ann and John Sugg created both a legal and environmental plan designed to last for generations. Their 852-acre legacy now provides an example for other private landowners who want to turn working farmland into protected natural areas while preserving the land for the future.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: Frogan breaks silence after Ethan Klein drops lawsuit as Twitch streamer questions whether legal fight is really over
articles.summary: US Streamers News: Twitch streamer Morgan “Frogan” has spoken out after Ethan Klein’s company voluntarily dismissed its copyright lawsuit against her. Court documents da.
articles.body: Twitch streamer Morgan “Frogan” has spoken out after Ethan Klein’s company voluntarily dismissed its copyright lawsuit against her. Court documents dated September 8, 2026, show that Ted Entertainment, Inc. dismissed the case without prejudice. That means the case has ended for now, but it can potentially be filed again. Frogan addressed the news on X the following day, saying she wanted to believe the decision meant the long legal fight was finally over. The lawsuit began in June 2025 after Klein accused Frogan, Denims and Kacey “Kaceytron” of violating his copyright by reacting to his video about Hasan Piker.Morgan “Frogan” reacts after Ethan Klein’s lawsuit is dismissedFrogan did not treat the dismissal as a complete victory because of the words “without prejudice.” In her September 9 X post, she explained that the lawsuit had taken a serious toll on her and said she hoped the latest court filing would finally bring the dispute to an end.“On September 8, 2026, I woke up to the news that Ethan Klein had voluntarily dismissed his lawsuit against me after more than a year,” Frogan wrote. She then pointed out that the dismissal could still allow the case to be filed again.“Of course, I want to be hopeful that it means the end of the lawsuit, which has taken an enormous toll on me,” she added. Frogan also repeated her position that her use of Klein’s video was protected by fair use and thanked the people who supported her during the case.The case goes back to June 2025. Klein filed copyright claims against Frogan, Denims and Kaceytron over their reactions to his YouTube video, “Content Nuke - Hasan Piker.” The legal dispute later took an unexpected turn in May 2026, when a court clerk entered a default against Frogan after her side failed to respond within the required time. A clerk’s default is a procedural step and is not automatically the same thing as a final judgment awarding the other side everything it requested.That distinction matters because reports at the time described the development as Klein winning against Frogan, while Frogan maintained that the case was not finished. The latest court filing now shows that Ted Entertainment chose to voluntarily dismiss the action without prejudice.Mike From PA comments on Ethan Klein’s legal dispute with FroganThe latest development also drew a reaction from streamer Michael “Mike From PA.” He criticized Klein’s handling of his legal disputes and claimed that the Frogan case was his fourth lawsuit lost in two years.“That's Ethan's 4th lawsuit he's lost in the last 2 years. He is still suing iDubbbz after promising to drop that lawsuit. Just how much money he's burned being humiliated in the courts?” Mike wrote.Those comments are Mike’s characterization of Klein’s legal record and should not be treated as a court finding. Public reporting shows that Klein has been involved in several legal disputes involving online creators. His separate dispute with iDubbbz also took a different path, with Klein saying he would drop that case after iDubbbz apologized.For Frogan, the immediate result is clear: Ted Entertainment has dismissed the copyright case against her without prejudice. She now has the outcome she had been waiting for, although the wording of the dismissal leaves open the possibility of another filing. As of September 10, 2026, no public statement from Ethan Klein explaining the decision had been reported.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. Download the TOI app.

articles.title: BJP to contest all 117 Punjab assembly seats alone, Satish Poonia says ‘no alliance’
articles.summary: JAISALMER: The BJP will contest all 117 Assembly seats in Punjab on its own in the upcoming elections, party national general secretary and Punjab in-.
articles.body: JAISALMER: The BJP will contest all 117 Assembly seats in Punjab on its own in the upcoming elections, party national general secretary and Punjab in-charge Satish Poonia said on Sunday.Speaking to reporters in Barmer, Poonia said the BJP would not be part of any alliance and would enter the electoral battle independently.During his one-day visit to Barmer, Poonia targeted the Aam Aadmi Party government over Punjab’s law and order situation and the drug menace. He said incidents of gang wars were being reported regularly and claimed that even AAP leaders had earlier fallen victim to such violence.He said Punjab needed a change and that the BJP would approach voters as an alternative to the present government.Poonia said the BJP had broken the perception in Haryana, Tripura and West Bengal that it could not come to power in these states. He said the party had traditionally contested Punjab elections in alliance, which limited the expansion of its organisation and its participation in government.Earlier, the BJP used to contest around 23 seats and win 12-13 of them. In 2022, it contested all 117 seats. Poonia said the central leadership and Punjab BJP unit had now decided to field candidates in all 117 constituencies in the coming election.Asked about the coincidence of Rajasthan Congress leader Sachin Pilot and Poonia being appointed in-charge of Punjab and Rajasthan respectively, Poonia said the matter could perhaps be explained only by an astrologer.In a lighter vein, he said both parties take their own decisions and do not act by looking at each other, calling it a coincidence that an astrologer could shed more light on.Poonia claimed that there was strong anti-incumbency against the AAP government, with three major issues — drugs, law and order and corruption.He said drugs had devastated Punjab’s youth, villages and families. Referring to cases of addiction, he said some families had lost multiple members to drugs.Poonia said Arvind Kejriwal had promised to eradicate drugs in Punjab within 90 days, but the problem continued even after nearly four-and-a-half years. He alleged that the drug menace had also fuelled gangster activities and gang wars, worsening the law and order situation.On corruption, Poonia levelled allegations against the government, including one concerning the Chief Minister’s wife and another involving an alleged attempt to protect a rape accused. He said drugs, law and order and corruption were the three major issues that would drive the BJP’s campaign against the AAP government.Poonia also announced that the BJP would organise an anti-drug awareness campaign in Punjab from September 18 to 30.The campaign will culminate in Jalandhar in the presence of Union Home Minister Amit Shah. Poonia said Shah had set a target of making the country drug-free by 2031.Poonia said he was confident in Shah’s resolve, citing the significant decline in Naxalism in the country as an example of the government fulfilling ambitious targets. He said Shah worked to fulfil the commitments he made.Poonia arrived in Barmer on a one-day visit. At the beginning of his tour, he visited Ramderiya at Oondu-Kashmir, regarded as the birthplace of folk deity Baba Ramdev, where he offered prayers and performed rituals.He later addressed a workers’ conference at the Barmer district BJP office.Before reaching Barmer, Poonia stopped at Phalsund in Jaisalmer district, where BJP leader Kanwaraj Singh, Gajrup Sagar Math Mahant Bal Bharti Maharaj and other local residents accorded him a warm welcome.You Can Also Check: Gold Rate in Jaipur | Silver Rate in Jaipur | Bank Holidays in Jaipur | Public Holidays in Jaipur | Jaipur AQI | Weather in Jaipur | Petrol Price in Jaipur | Diesel Price in Jaipur | CNG Price in Jaipur | LPG Price in JaipurStay updated with the latest Jaipur news. articles.title: In 2018, an unbuilt penthouse shell under Manhattan's Hampshire House roof was marketed at $40 million; eight years later, it found a buyer at $6.765 million, 83% below the ask
articles.summary: Real Estate News: An unfinished penthouse space inside one of the most famous buildings on Manhattan’s Billionaires’ Row has found a buyer for $6.765 million. The sale .
articles.body: An unfinished penthouse space inside one of the most famous buildings on Manhattan’s Billionaires’ Row has found a buyer for $6.765 million. The sale represents an 83 percent drop from the $40 million asking price placed on the raw space eight years ago. According to the listing and auction details, the three-level property is located beneath the steep copper roof of Hampshire House at 150 Central Park South. It went under contract after a competitive online auction. The heavily reduced sale price brings an end, at least for now, to a long-running real estate story that shows the risks involved in expensive and highly ambitious luxury developments in New York City.From Grand Vision to Market RealityAccording to property marketing materials, the unfinished attic space first went on the market in 2018 with a $40 million asking price. It was presented as a rare opportunity for someone to create a custom home overlooking Central Park. Pre-approved architectural plans from SPAN Architecture were included to help potential buyers understand what could be built. The plans called for a 9,000-square-foot triplex with five bedrooms, five-and-a-half bathrooms, and four private outdoor terraces covering 1,200 square feet. One of the most unusual features in the proposed design was a glass-covered rooftop walkway with a wet bar. It was planned to run between the building’s two famous copper chimneys. According to Interior Design Magazine, the proposed design received a Best of Year award even though it existed only on paper. Despite the attention surrounding the project, finding a buyer willing to take on the huge construction costs proved very difficult.Major Construction Costs Created a BarrierThe biggest challenge was that the property had almost no finished interior infrastructure. Instead of buying a completed luxury apartment, the buyer was essentially purchasing a large empty attic that would need extensive construction. Early property estimates said turning the space into a basic finished interior would take between 18 and 24 months of major construction. Marketing materials also estimated that completing the full design would cost another $15 million to $20 million on top of the purchase price. The work was made even more difficult because it had to be carried out inside a historic pre-war co-op building. Potential buyers also had to pass the Hampshire House co-op board’s strict financial and background approval process. According to the property’s sales history, the space went through several different marketing strategies over the years. After failing to sell for $40 million, it was removed from the market and later listed again for $18.75 million. It was eventually offered through an auction run by Concierge Auctions in partnership with Nest Seekers International.Historic Architectural BackgroundEven with its dramatic price reduction, the penthouse remains one of the most unusual residential spaces in New York City. Hampshire House has a long and complicated architectural history. According to historical records, construction on the 39-story building began in 1926 as a project called Medici Tower, led by developer Eugene Lignante. The project stopped after the Wall Street Crash of 1929, leaving its steel frame standing above Central Park for almost a decade. The development was later revived and completed between 1937 and 1940 by architects Caughey & Evans. They added the steep copper roof and detailed white-brick exterior that make the building easy to recognise today. Renowned interior designer Dorothy Draper designed the building’s grand lobby, helping establish Hampshire House as a prestigious address. Over the years, the building has been home to a number of well-known residents, including famous opera tenor Luciano Pavarotti.Auction Process Produces a Final SaleAccording to Concierge Auctions, the final sale followed a competitive online auction. Bidding started at $6 million before ending at $6.765 million. Auction officials said that although the final price was far below the original expectations, the auction process helped reveal what buyers were actually willing to pay for such an unusual property. Chad Roffers, chief executive and co-founder of Concierge Auctions, said the result showed the value of using a clear and competitive auction process for rare properties. “This sale demonstrates that truly irreplaceable real estate continues to command global attention when presented through a transparent, time-defined process,” Roffers said. “The Hampshire House penthouse represents one of the rarest residential offerings in New York City, a hidden architectural landmark with remarkable redevelopment potential.” The new owner will still face a difficult and expensive construction project before the proposed plans can become a real home. However, the sale finally creates an opportunity for one of Manhattan’s most famous unused spaces to be transformed into a finished residence.Ready to Make a Smarter Property Decision? articles.body: US president Donald Trump on Monday demanded that countries benefiting from the security of the Strait of Hormuz reimburse Washington for the costs of protecting the crucial oil-shipping route, accusing nations of providing “no help whatsoever” during the conflict with Iran.In a series of posts on Truth Social, Trump said oil was continuing to flow through the strategic waterway and argued that the United States should be compensated once the military conflict ends.“Oil is flowing through the Hormuz Strait. The Countries of the World, which have been no help to us whatsoever, should, and will, reimburse the United States of America when this SCAM Confligration is all over,” Trump wrote.“We are doing it much more for others, than we are for ourselves, and we have been for Generations!”, the US president added.Meanwhile, Tehran asserts control over the strategic waterway and maintains restrictions on shipping. Iranian officials have said that vessels must follow routes and procedures set by Tehran, while Washington has rejected Iran’s claim to control the strait.Trump’s demand came as the US military continued efforts to keep oil shipments moving through the waterway. Earlier on Monday, energy secretary Chris Wright told reporters that the number of oil shipments escorted by the US Navy through Hormuz was increasing on average, according to Reuters.Trump has repeatedly sought to portray the US military campaign against Iran as a success. He has claimed that Washington has already won the war, destroyed Iran’s military and “obliterated” its nuclear programme, even as US military officials have raised concerns about depleted arsenals and overstretched ships at sea.Trump also sought to shift responsibility for higher prices in the US away from his administration, blaming former President Joe Biden for inflation and elevated oil prices.In another post, he wrote, “I hope everyone realizes that price increases throughout America were caused by Sleepy Joe Biden and the Biden Administration, not by “TRUMP.” Even Oil was higher under Biden than it is right now, and we prevented Iran from having a Nuclear Weapon!”THe claimed that the oil prices would “drop like a rock” once the Iran conflict ends, which he expects to happen soon. Earlier on Monday, Trump had also indicated that Tehran was seeking negotiations.“The failing Nation of Iran wants to make a deal, quickly and badly. I will determine whether or not the USA. will choose to engage - The concept of which we are open to,” Trump wrote.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. Download the TOI app.

articles.title: Scientists planted 150,650 native koa trees on Hawaii’s abandoned pasture, but 20 years later endangered birds were moving into the young forest
articles.summary: US News: For decades, cattle had grazed across large areas of what is now Hakalau Forest National Wildlife Refuge on Hawaii's Big Island, leaving thousands of .
articles.body: For decades, cattle had grazed across large areas of what is now Hakalau Forest National Wildlife Refuge on Hawaii's Big Island, leaving thousands of acres dominated by pasture grasses instead of native forest. Then, beginning in the 1990s, conservationists began rebuilding the forest one tree at a time. Between 1992 and 1996, American Forests supported the planting of 150,650 native koa trees across degraded pasture at Hakalau. The aim was not simply to put trees back on the landscape. The young forest was intended to create habitat and nesting areas for some of Hawaii's rarest birds.Two decades later, researchers found that the strategy was working. Birds that depended on native forest were moving into the restored areas, with several species increasing as the planted trees matured. A later study using more than 20 years of observations described the Hakalau project as one of the largest ongoing reforestation efforts in Hawaii and found that time since restoration and proximity to intact forest strongly influenced how quickly birds colonised the new woodland.American Forests planted 150,650 koa trees across abandoned pastureHakalau Forest National Wildlife Refuge covers roughly 34,000 acres on the slopes of Mauna Kea and contains some of the last extensive montane rainforest habitat in Hawaii. But much of the landscape had been transformed by cattle ranching. American Forests says that thousands of acres inside the refuge had become abandoned pasture, with invasive weeds and grasses replacing the native vegetation. From 1992 to 1996, the organisation supported the planting of 150,650 koa trees, a native Hawaiian tree considered a keystone species in these forests.The project built on earlier restoration work that began in the refuge in the 1980s. The idea was to establish strips and corridors of native trees through the open pasture, creating a bridge between surviving forest and areas where native vegetation had disappeared. Koa was particularly useful because it could grow relatively quickly on degraded land while providing structure and resources that could eventually support other native plants and animals.The 2003 paper ‘Tree Planting at Hakalau Forest National Wildlife Refuge, the Right Tool for the Right Stock Type,’ published in Native Plants Journal, was written by Jack Jeffrey and Baron Horiuchi. The researchers described koa and ‘ōhi‘a lehua as important species for restoring degraded parts of Hakalau and explained how different planting tools were used for different types of seedlings.The young forest was designed to bring endangered Hawaiian birds backThe trees were never the only goal. Hakalau was established in 1985 specifically to provide habitat for rare and endangered native forest birds. But much of the upper refuge had already been heavily altered by ranching, leaving large areas of open pasture where forest birds could no longer find the food, shelter and nesting habitat they needed.The restoration corridors were therefore intended to do more than replace missing trees. They were designed to create foraging cover, nesting sites and food resources while helping native forest gradually expand into former pasture. Koa also had an important ecological advantage. Its canopy could eventually shade out some of the aggressive pasture grasses while creating a more forest-like environment beneath the trees. That could make conditions more suitable for the return of native understory plants.American Forests says endangered birds including the ‘i‘iwi, or scarlet honeycreeper, and the ‘akiapōlā‘au began returning to areas that had once been largely barren. The organisation describes the project as one of the world's notable examples of native forest restoration. The restoration was therefore conceived as a long-term ecological transition: plant native trees first, allow the canopy to develop, then create the conditions in which a more complex native forest community could return.After more than 20 years, birds began colonising the planted forestThe strongest evidence of what happened next came from researchers who examined the bird community over a much longer period. In the study ‘Predicting effects of large-scale reforestation on native and exotic birds,’ published in Diversity and Distributions, Liba Pejchar, Travis Gallo, Mevin Hooten and Gretchen C. Daily examined a reforestation project at Hakalau that was already more than 20 years old. Their research asked how quickly a landscape converted from pasture to young native forest could begin supporting forest birds.The researchers surveyed birds in several types of habitat, including corridors of young planted trees, remnants of mature forest and mature forest itself. They found that time since restoration and distance from intact forest were important predictors of bird abundance and colonisation. That meant the young forest was not immediately equivalent to old-growth forest. Birds did not all arrive at the same speed, and species farther from existing forest generally took longer to colonise the restored areas. But the direction was clear: as the planted forest developed, native birds increasingly used it.A separate long-term study, 'Rapid colonization of a Hawaiian restoration forest by a diverse avian community,' analysed 26 years of bird-count data at Hakalau. The researchers found that most species in the diverse forest-bird community increased significantly in the restoration forest, although different species colonised at different rates.Endangered birds were using trees planted on former cattle pastureThe results were particularly significant because Hawaii has lost much of its original forest and many of its endemic birds are found nowhere else on Earth. The long-term Hakalau research showed that restoration could provide useful habitat even before a planted forest had reached the structure of mature native woodland. Forest cover and the diversity of vegetation beneath the trees also helped explain bird densities.Some species responded relatively quickly, while others took much longer to appear. The ‘akiapōlā‘au, an endangered Hawaiian honeycreeper, was among the species recorded in the restoration forest and showed an increasing trend over the study period. That gradual colonisation matters because Hawaiian forest birds face threats beyond habitat loss. Introduced mosquitoes and avian malaria have devastated many native species, while invasive plants and animals continue to alter their remaining habitat.Hakalau's restoration therefore offers more than a simple tree-planting success story. The young forest provides an expanding refuge at higher elevations, where conservationists hope native birds can find enough habitat to persist as environmental conditions change. American Forests is now involved in another stage of that effort. Its Kanakaleonui Bird Corridor project aims to connect Hakalau with higher-elevation forests on Mauna Kea, potentially giving vulnerable birds access to cooler habitat as climate change pushes mosquitoes and avian malaria into areas that were once relatively safe.The story of Hakalau began with a landscape altered by more than a century of cattle grazing. In the 1990s, conservationists planted 150,650 native trees across part of that abandoned pasture. More than 20 years later, researchers were documenting forest birds moving through the young woodland. The trees did not recreate an ancient forest overnight. Instead, they provided the first structure from which a new forest could grow, and, with it, a route back for some of Hawaii's most threatened birds.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: India to supply Nepal electricity after floods wrecked hydropower projects
articles.summary: India to provide Nepal with 654 megawatts of electricity daily to meet urgent needs after devastating glacial floods.
articles.body:
India has approved the expedited export of 654 megawatts of electricity to Nepal for 18 hours per day until December 31 to help the country overcome power shortages caused by extensive flood damage to hydropower infrastructure.

The devastating floods in Nepal, triggered by a glacial mountain collapse on the China-Nepal border, killed over 1,400 people, damaged at least 12 hydropower projects, and left more than 5,500 people missing, forcing the country to import electricity after years of exporting surplus energy to India.

The United Nations and its partners are appealing for nearly $50m to help survivors of the floods in Nepal, with officials estimating that at least $5bn is needed for initial rebuilding, highlighting the impact of climate change on poor countries like Nepal.

India has approved the expedited export of electricity to neighbouring Nepal to help it overcome shortages caused by extensive damage to hydropower infrastructure from devastating floods last month.

In a statement on Monday, India's Ministry of Power said up to 654 megawatts of electricity would be transmitted for 18 hours per day until December 31.

"The approval will help Nepal meet its power requirements during this difficult period and further strengthen the close and longstanding energy cooperation between India and Nepal," it said.

It added that in December it would also review the amount of power to be exported from January.

The flooding , triggered on August 26 by a glacial mountain collapse on the China-Nepal border, killed more than 1,400 people in Nepal and Tibet.

At least 12 hydropower projects in Nepal were hit, with at least 900 power station workers among the more than 5,500 people still missing in the country.

Almost 100 percent of the country's energy needs were met by hydropower before the floods hit. Since then, Nepal has been forced to import electricity after years of exporting surplus energy to India.

Thousands of displaced people are sheltering in aid centres, with little hope of returning home soon. The United Nations and its partners are appealing for nearly $50m to help survivors.

Nepali officials say at least $5bn is needed for initial rebuilding, adding that the disaster shows how climate change has hit poor countries that did little to cause it.

The ‌Himalayas, where Nepal is nestled, are approaching a tipping point as glaciers melt ⁠faster than a decade ⁠ago, threatening water security as the region approaches "peak water" by mid-century, according to a study released this month.

articles.title: In 1835, Free Frank McWorter, a formerly enslaved man, paid $100 for 80 Illinois acres; a year later he founded New Philadelphia, and 191 years later nearly 20 acres entered NPS ownership
articles.summary: US News: Nearly two centuries after a formerly enslaved pioneer bought 80 acres of Illinois prairie and founded the first legally registered town in the United.
articles.body: Nearly two centuries after a formerly enslaved pioneer bought 80 acres of Illinois prairie and founded the first legally registered town in the United States platted by an African American, nearly 20 acres of the historic townsite have officially been transferred to the National Park Service.According to the National Park Service, the land was donated by the nonprofit New Philadelphia Association and is an important addition to the New Philadelphia National Historic Site. Located near Barry in Pike County, the site protects the story of Free Frank McWorter, who established an integrated frontier community decades before the American Civil War. The acquisition protects important visitor facilities and historic land, helping preserve the story of self-emancipation, cooperation between Black and white residents, and pioneer determination for future generations.From bondage to pioneer landownershipAccording to National Park Service historical information, New Philadelphia began with the determination of Frank McWorter, who was born into slavery in South Carolina in 1777. While living in Kentucky, McWorter was allowed to operate saltpetre mining businesses alongside his forced labor. By carefully saving his earnings, he was able to buy the freedom of his wife, Lucy, in 1817. He purchased his own freedom two years later. In 1830, McWorter moved his family to Illinois. According to historical accounts, Illinois allowed free Black people to purchase property under federal land laws, despite strict state limits on their civil rights. Five years later, in 1835, McWorter paid $100 for an 80-acre piece of federal land in rural Pike County. According to the National Park Service, McWorter saw an opportunity to build a town in the area. In 1836, he set aside 42 acres of his property and divided it into 144 residential and commercial lots. He then formally created the town of New Philadelphia. This made him the first African American in U.S. history known to legally establish and register a municipality.A community built on lot salesMcWorter’s plans went beyond buying and selling land. According to the New Philadelphia National Historic Site, he designed the community as an integrated and affordable place where Black and white families could own property, run businesses, and educate their children. Money from the sale of town lots helped fund McWorter’s main goal: buying his family members out of slavery. According to historical records, McWorter used money from his Illinois land transactions to purchase the freedom of 16 relatives, including children, grandchildren, and his mother. The total cost was about $14,000. During the years before the Civil War, New Philadelphia also became part of the Underground Railroad. According to the National Park Service, the town’s location between the Mississippi and Illinois rivers allowed local residents to help enslaved people escaping from nearby Missouri as they travelled north toward Canada. By the late 1860s, the town had about 160 residents. Historical records show that the community included blacksmith shops, general stores, a wheelwright, and an integrated public school.Railroad bypass, decline, and archaeological rediscoveryThe decline of New Philadelphia followed a pattern seen in many Midwestern towns during the late 19th century. According to the National Park Service, the Hannibal and Naples Railroad bypassed the town in 1869 and instead built its tracks through nearby Barry. Without access to the new railroad, businesses and residents slowly moved away. By the 1920s, the town’s original buildings had disappeared, and the land had returned largely to agricultural use. Although the buildings were gone, much of New Philadelphia’s history remained underground. According to information from the New Philadelphia Association and archaeological researchers, local residents formed the association in the late 1990s to protect the historic site from highway construction and damage caused by farming. Archaeologists from the University of Illinois and other institutions later carried out major excavations. They found thousands of household objects, road remains, and building foundations. The discoveries helped lead to New Philadelphia being added to the National Register of Historic Places in 2005. The site was later named a National Historic Landmark in 2009.National park status and partnership milestonesAccording to the National Park Service, Congress officially added New Philadelphia to the National Park System in December 2022, making it the 424th unit of the system. Since then, federal officials have worked with local community groups to acquire important parcels within the park’s 124-acre boundary. The recent donation of nearly 20 acres by the New Philadelphia Association transfers ownership of the park’s main public access area. According to the National Park Service, the property includes an information kiosk, educational displays, accessible parking, and other cultural features created with help from local volunteers. New Philadelphia National Historic Site Superintendent Chris Collins said the partnership with the local association has been important to the park’s development. “This donation is an important step in protecting the resources and stories of New Philadelphia for the community and visitors,” Collins said. “Our partnership with the New Philadelphia Association has been essential to the park's development. I am excited to continue working alongside our partners as we plan for the future of New Philadelphia National Historic Site.” With the land now under National Park Service ownership, federal officials are working on long-term plans for visitor education, improved trails, and archaeological preservation. According to the National Park Service, these efforts will help protect and explain Free Frank McWorter’s lasting legacy on the Illinois prairie.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: Meet Meera Ramaswami: The Ann Arbor inventor who turned her grandmother’s fall into a patented mobility device and launched a company
articles.summary: US News: A fall while getting out of a car changed the direction of Meera Ramaswami’s life. She watched her grandmother lose her balance during a moment that s.
articles.body: A fall while getting out of a car changed the direction of Meera Ramaswami’s life. She watched her grandmother lose her balance during a moment that should have been routine, then saw the injury heal while the fear remained. Her grandmother became less willing to travel, and Meera began thinking about how a small loss of stability could lead to isolation and lost independence. That question eventually became Cargility, an Ann Arbor company developing a portable mobility aid that helps people enter and exit vehicles safely. Meera designed the device, tested prototypes, earned recognition through The Henry Ford’s Invention Convention and secured a US utility patent. As reported by The Henry Ford and Ann Arbor SPARK, the invention has grown from a family experience into a company founded by Meera and her mother, Praveena Ramaswami.A familiar moment with serious consequencesGetting into or out of a car is an ordinary action for most people, but it can become difficult after an injury, during ageing or for anyone with balance and mobility challenges. A person may need to twist, lower themselves, find a stable surface and stand on uneven ground, all while managing the distance between the seat and pavement.For Meera’s grandmother, that moment led to a fall. The physical injury eventually healed, but the emotional effect lasted longer. Fear of falling again changed how willing she was to leave home. A simple vehicle transfer became a barrier to travel, social connection and independence.Meera recognised that the problem was larger than one family. Older adults, people recovering from surgery or rehabilitation, people with disabilities and caregivers may all face difficulties during vehicle entry and exit. Existing solutions such as walking frames, canes or assistance from another person may not be convenient in the narrow space beside a car. Observation to design Meera began developing the concept in 2022, using a process of observation, prototyping and testing. She didn’t start with an abstract engineering problem, but rather looked at a specific moment in everyday life and asked what kind of support would make it safer. The device needed to be portable, strong and compatible with different passenger vehicles. It also had to be easy enough for a user or caregiver to position without complicated installation. A support that worked only in one type of car would have limited value, so adaptability became an important part of the design.The resulting product, Cargility, is a door to floor mobility assistive device. It engages with the striker in a vehicle’s doorframe and creates a stable support point. An articulating leg reaches the ground, allowing the user to lean on a railing while entering or exiting the vehicle.The design is intended to reduce fall risk and ease the physical strain placed on caregivers. It provides a fixed point of support during the transfer rather than requiring a person to rely on a moving car door or another individual’s strength.How the device worksThe Cargility tool is designed to connect with the striker plate, the metal component in the vehicle doorframe that receives the door latch. Once engaged, the device holds a stable relationship to the vehicle. Its articulating leg consists of two members connected by a pivot, so that the structure can accommodate various vehicle heights and configurations. When positioned correctly, the leg reaches the ground and supports a handrail or bar that the user can hold.The aim is to create a continuous point of stability between the vehicle and the ground. A person can use the rail while lowering into the seat or standing up, reducing the need to twist quickly or search for something to grip.The tool is not intended to replace a doctor, physical therapist or properly prescribed mobility aid. Its purpose is to make one specific part of everyday movement safer and more manageable. The device would still need to be attached correctly and users need to follow the instructions before they can rely on it. Testing and refining the inventionDeveloping the first concept was only the beginning. Meera tested different designs and compared their performance. Earlier descriptions of her work indicate that she created possible models, evaluated them and selected the design that performed best.This kind of testing is central to invention education. A promising idea may fail when exposed to weight, movement, different surfaces or different vehicle shapes.Prototypes expose weaknesses that aren’t apparent on paper. Meera’s work also involved a balancing act between conflicting requirements. The device had to be strong enough to hold a person, but portable enough to carry. It had to fit different cars, but be stable. It had to be easy for users, but not compromise safety. The process required engineering knowledge, but also empathy.A technically impressive device would not be useful if older adults or caregivers found it too complicated. Designing for real people meant considering reach, grip, balance, strength and confidence.Recognition through The Henry FordMeera’s invention gained recognition through the Invention Convention, a programme supported by The Henry Ford that encourages young people to identify problems and develop solutions. The programme teaches students to move through stages including constructing a prototype, testing it, revising the design and communicating the final idea.In 2022, Meera received top honours in four engineering categories at the Invention Convention held at the Henry Ford Museum.Those awards included innovation, safety, Make the World and the Grand Prize, which provided support for bringing the invention to the US Patent Office.The recognition helped Meera to validate the invention and gain access to a network of mentors, educators and organizations experienced in product development. It also helped turn the project from a student design into an innovation with commercial potential.For young inventors, programmes like the Invention Convention can provide something that classrooms often cannot. They offer a structured way to develop an idea, receive feedback and present it to people who understand engineering and entrepreneurship.From invention to patentCargility’s mobility concept eventually became a patented technology.Meera Ramaswami was awarded the US patent “Vehicle Access Mobility Tool” in December 2025. The patent describes a device that latches to a vehicle doorframe striker and has an articulating leg attached to the engagement portion. A patent does not mean a product is ready for mass production or on store shelves. It protects the claimed invention and establishes intellectual property rights. It was a major milestone, but more work is needed to make the patented design a reliable product, including manufacturing, testing, regulatory considerations, supply chains and consumer input. It showed that the device had moved beyond a school project and into a formal innovation process. It also created a foundation for building a company around the technology.A mother and daughter become co-foundersMeera did not build the company alone. She and her mother, Praveena Ramaswami, became co-founders of Cargility in 2025. Meera continued developing the technical solution, while Praveena left her career to focus full time on the business.The partnership combines engineering and commercial development. Meera understands the design and the problem that inspired it. Praveena has focused on evaluating the mobility ecosystem, building relationships and determining how the company can move toward manufacturing and customers. Starting a company for a physical product is not just having an invention. Founders need to find users, understand the healthcare and mobility market, figure out a pricing model, and decide how the device will be distributed. They must also test the product with the people it is meant to help.The mother daughter structure gives Cargility a personal connection to its mission. The company exists because a family experienced the emotional consequences of a fall and decided to look for a better way.The wider need for mobility supportCargility is aimed at people who may need additional stability during vehicle transfers. That includes older adults, people recovering from rehabilitation and caregivers who help family members get in and out of cars.Vehicle transfers are often overlooked in discussions about accessibility. Public buildings may have ramps and lifts, but the journey begins at home and frequently includes the space between a car seat and the ground. A person may be able to walk once standing but still struggle with the transition.A portable device could be useful for people who travel in different vehicles or do not want permanent equipment installed. It may also help caregivers avoid lifting or pulling, reducing strain on both people.The product’s success will depend on real world testing and user trust. People need confidence that a device will remain secure, work on their vehicle and support them when balance is uncertain.Building an Ann Arbor companyCargility is part of Ann Arbor’s expanding technology and entrepreneurship ecosystem. The city has programmes that connect founders with mentors, accelerators, university resources and funding opportunities. Ann Arbor SPARK has supported founders through initiatives including Entrepreneur Boot Camp, startup acceleration and other business programmes.For Cargility, that ecosystem can help bridge the gap between invention and commercial launch. Product development may require industrial designers, manufacturing partners, safety experts and investors. Local programmes can connect a small founding team with people who have experience in each area.The company has advanced to a working prototype with design for manufacturing completed and has been targeting an initial small production run and market launch. That stage is important because the best prototype is not always the easiest product to manufacture consistently. A design for manufacturing review helps identify ways to reduce complexity, control cost and maintain quality.A personal problem becomes a public solutionMeera’s story began with a private family moment, but the problem she identified is widely shared. Falls can change how older adults and people with mobility limitations view daily activities. Fear can lead to fewer outings, less social contact and greater dependence on others.The Cargility device cannot remove every risk associated with movement. It can, however, address one vulnerable transition with a practical support. The invention shows how innovation often begins when someone pays close attention to an ordinary problem that others have accepted as unavoidable.Its future will depend on continued testing, responsible manufacturing and feedback from users. But the path from grandmother’s fall to patent and company already demonstrates the power of human centred design.Meera did not begin with the intention of becoming a founder. She began by wanting to make one moment safer for someone she loved. That empathy became an engineering question, the question became a prototype and the prototype became Cargility, an Ann Arbor company working to help people move with greater confidence and independence.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: A US grandfather planned a $100,000-$150,000 treehouse for his grandkids; it grew into a $325,000 backyard castle with a pirate ship and 200-foot zipline
articles.summary: US News: What started as a simple plan to build a cozy backyard play area for his grandchildren grew into an impressive architectural project after an American.
articles.body: What started as a simple plan to build a cozy backyard play area for his grandchildren grew into an impressive architectural project after an American grandfather expanded the idea into a $325,000 custom treehouse complex. According to the Realtor.com, the original budget was between $100,000 and $150,000 for a basic structure. But as new ideas were added, the project continued to grow. Today, the unusual installation looks like a fairytale playground hidden among the trees, complete with a full-size pirate ship and a 200-foot zipline running across the property. The size and detail of the project have turned a private family backyard into a remarkable example of a grandfather’s dedication, combining skilled carpentry with childhood imagination.A modest plan that grew far beyond its budgetThe original idea was fairly simple. The owner wanted to build a strong, raised play structure where his grandchildren could spend summer afternoons outdoors. But during the early design process, the project quickly became much more ambitious. Instead of choosing a standard wooden platform, the homeowner worked with custom builders to add special architectural features. What began as a small cabin developed into a multi-level structure with sloping roofs, finished loft spaces, custom windows, live-edge cedar siding, and hand-cut cedar shingles. As more features were added, the estimated cost increased sharply. According to the project details, the final price reached $325,000 after high-quality materials, structural engineering reviews, and safety features were included.High-flying features and a pirate ship extensionThe main part of the complex is a 12-foot-by-12-foot treehouse raised high above the ground. A tall lookout tower rises above the roof and gives visitors wide views of the surrounding garden. The main treehouse was first connected to a separate wooden platform by an open-air rope bridge. However, the owner decided that a simple observation deck was not exciting enough for his growing grandchildren. The second platform was then rebuilt and turned into a large pirate ship extension. According to the project details, it includes play cannons, nautical ropes and equipment, and wooden decks designed around the pirate theme. For even more adventure, an octagonal launch platform was built beside the main treehouse. From there, riders can attach themselves to a 200-foot zipline that carries them through the trees to a special landing tower inspired by Rapunzel’s castle.Expert engineering keeps the play area safeBuilding such a large treehouse required more than basic do-it-yourself skills. Custom treehouse engineers were brought in to make sure the structures were safe for children and did not damage the trees supporting them. According to Tree Top Builders, the company involved in creating the aerial design, “Building a treehouse is easy, but building a safe, long-lasting, tree-friendly treehouse requires expertise.” The company also said, “We work with the tree, not against it.” Arborists and structural engineers worked together to create flexible attachment systems. These systems allow the trees to move naturally during strong winds and continue growing without being restricted by heavy support beams. According to the project information, the interiors were finished with smooth wooden walls and strong safety railings, creating a secure space for children to use throughout the year.A fairytale legacy for future generationsAlthough the final cost was much higher than the original budget, the project created a unique family space that has become a centerpiece for gatherings. The $325,000 backyard treehouse is more than an elaborate playground. According to the project details, it was designed to remain useful as the grandchildren grow into teenagers and young adults. The finished lofts provide flexible areas for relaxing and spending time together, while the strong construction is designed to keep the complex standing for many years. What began as a simple backyard project has therefore become a lasting family attraction, combining adventure, craftsmanship, and a grandfather’s desire to create something special for future generations.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: Sweden imported 2.5 million tonnes of European waste and treated it to produce heat and electricity for over a million apartments
articles.summary: Rest of World News: Sweden processed 2.5 million tonnes of sorted waste imported from other European countries in 2024. The country’s waste-to-energy plants have more cap.
articles.body: Sweden processed 2.5 million tonnes of sorted waste imported from other European countries in 2024. The country’s waste-to-energy plants have more capacity than the amount of combustible waste generated within Sweden, which allows them to accept waste from abroad. Avfall Sverige’s Swedish Waste Management 2024 report states that 1.2 million tonnes of the imported waste were municipal waste. The imported material provided fuel for energy recovery while helping other European countries deal with their waste. Swedish energy recovery plants handled 6.6 million tonnes of waste during the year and generated about 20 terawatt-hours of energy. This included 17.6 TWh used for heating and 2.4 TWh for electricity.Why did Sweden import 2.5 million tonnes of waste in 2024 from EuropeSweden has more energy recovery capacity than the amount of combustible waste generated domestically, allowing its plants to accept waste from other European countries. In 2024, Swedish facilities treated 2.5 million tonnes of sorted European waste, including 1.2 million tonnes of municipal waste. The imported waste became part of the fuel used by these energy recovery plants. Avfall Sverige also notes that accepting waste from abroad can help exporting countries manage waste that might otherwise require other forms of treatment. The report places this practice within Europe’s wider move away from landfill, as countries look for alternative ways to treat waste and recover value from discarded materials.How Sweden turned 6.6 million tonnes of waste into energyEnergy recovery was used to treat waste that should not be handled through other methods. Swedish plants received 6.6 million tonnes of waste for energy recovery in 2024. Household waste made up 1.9 million tonnes, or 28% of the total, while waste from companies and industries accounted for the remaining 72%. These plants recovered around 20 terawatt-hours of energy from the waste. Heating received the largest share at 17.6 TWh, while 2.4 TWh was converted into electricity. Five plants also reported supplying 0.1 TWh of district cooling. The report describes energy recovery as a hygienic and sound way to treat waste that cannot be handled through other methods.Waste-to-energy plants helped power more than 940,000 Swedish apartmentsWaste energy recovery made a significant contribution to Sweden’s heating and electricity supply in 2024. The energy recovered from waste was enough to heat more than 1,470,000 apartments and provide electricity for over 940,000 apartments. Swedish plants recovered around 3.0 megawatt-hours of energy per tonne of waste, placing the country among Europe’s leading waste-to-energy performers by energy recovery per tonne. Heating accounted for the largest share at 17.6 terawatt-hours, while electricity generation produced 2.4 TWh. Together, the two forms of energy counted about 20 TWh.How Sweden manages slag and ash left after waste incinerationEnergy recovery does not remove all material from the waste. Incineration leaves behind residues such as slag, bottom ash and flue gas treatment residues. In 2024, slag and bottom ash totalled 914,820 tonnes, while flue gas treatment residues reached 299,650 tonnes. Slag contains non-combustible materials including glass, porcelain, iron scrap and gravel. Once metals are separated, the remaining material can be processed into granulated slag. According to the report, this material is largely used as a construction material at landfill sites. Using granulated slag in place of natural sand and gravel could also reduce the need to extract these finite resources for uses where they are still required.Why fossil plastics remain a challenge for waste-to-energy plantsWaste sent for energy recovery can contain fossil-based plastics and other materials that cannot be recycled, along with packaging that ends up in residual waste. Burning these materials releases fossil carbon dioxide. The report aims to halve fossil emissions from energy recovery by 2030 and bring them close to zero by 2045. In 2022, 136 million tonnes of waste were sent to landfill across the EU, including 51 million tonnes of municipal waste. The report places Sweden’s waste imports within a broader move to reduce landfill use and recover energy from waste that cannot be managed through other treatment methods.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: In 1990, mining stopped at a 55-metre-deep Swedish limestone quarry; a year later, an opera singer discovered its remarkable natural sound, and it became Dalhalla, now drawing 100,000+ visitors each summer
articles.summary: Rest of World News: When mining stopped at an isolated limestone quarry in central Sweden in 1990, the local area was left with a 55-metre-deep industrial pit cut into th.
articles.body: When mining stopped at an isolated limestone quarry in central Sweden in 1990, the local area was left with a 55-metre-deep industrial pit cut into the pine forests outside Rättvik. Just a year later, a former opera singer discovered that the abandoned quarry had remarkable natural acoustics. Today, the former mining site has become Dalhalla, an internationally known open-air concert venue that attracts more than 100,000 music fans to Dalarna every summer.A geological crater shaped by an ancient impactAccording to geological information about the area, the site that became Dalhalla was shaped by a huge meteorite impact around 360 million years ago. A meteorite about four kilometres wide struck the Earth and created the geological formation now known as the Siljan Ring. The impact changed the local rock formations, bringing ancient layers of limestone closer to the surface. According to historical accounts of the quarry, commercial mining began at the Dräggängarna site in the 1940s, with companies removing millions of tonnes of limestone over several decades. When mining finally stopped in 1990, workers had created a huge natural bowl about 400 metres long, 175 metres wide, and 55 metres deep. According to information about the site, underground springs had also begun filling the bottom of the quarry, creating a bright turquoise lake. The colour comes from dissolved calcium carbonate in the water, which reflects the northern sunlight.The Whitsun walk that sparked a visionThe quarry might have remained an abandoned industrial site if not for a walk taken during Pentecost in 1991. According to accounts of Dalhalla’s history, Margareta Dellefors, a former Swedish opera singer and radio producer, was searching for an outdoor location for a new summer music festival. When Dellefors reached the edge of the abandoned quarry, she looked across the huge open space and tested its acoustics by calling her voice across the pit. She was surprised by how clear and powerful the sound was. According to accounts of the discovery, the quarry produced strong natural resonance without creating harsh echoes. Dellefors quickly saw the potential for a concert venue. The shape of the quarry was also considered suitable for an outdoor theatre, while its limestone walls helped spread and soften sound across the basin. The venue was eventually named Dalhalla. According to the venue’s history, the name combines Dalarna, the region where it is located, with Valhalla, the great hall from Norse mythology that also became famous through Richard Wagner’s operas.From acoustic test to national landmarkTurning an abandoned quarry into a working concert venue required major construction and engineering work. According to Dalhalla’s history, Dellefors worked with local authorities to remove debris, create access routes down the quarry walls, and build a permanent stage beside the lake. In June 1993, organisers held a test concert for invited journalists, acoustics experts, and local residents. The performance showed that classical music could be heard clearly throughout the quarry, confirming the site’s unusual acoustic qualities. The venue officially opened to the public on June 21, 1995, with a major opera performance that was broadcast nationally by Swedish Television. According to historical accounts, the television broadcast introduced Dalhalla to a much wider Swedish audience and helped establish the former quarry as an important cultural destination.Overcoming environmental and staging challengesRunning a large outdoor venue inside a 55-metre-deep quarry creates several practical challenges. According to information from Dalhalla, the stage is located well below the surrounding forest. Performers, equipment, and other supplies therefore have to be moved through steep access routes built into the rock. The quarry also has its own small-scale climate conditions. Its deep walls help protect the performance area from strong winds and outside noise, but changes in temperature and humidity can affect how sound moves through the air. To protect the site and improve the visitor experience, managers installed systems to control the level of the central lake. Electrical equipment was also placed carefully along the rock face. According to descriptions of the venue, this allows modern lighting systems to illuminate the limestone walls during evening shows while keeping the natural appearance of the quarry.A wide range of music attracts visitors from around the worldDalhalla was originally created mainly for opera and classical music. However, according to the venue’s programme history, its schedule gradually expanded to include many different styles of music. Over the past three decades, the amphitheatre has hosted symphony orchestras, ballet groups, jazz performers, and major pop and rock artists. International performers have appeared in front of the illuminated limestone walls, with many praising the unusual setting and atmosphere. The summer season, which runs from late spring into early autumn, includes dozens of performances. According to information about the venue, these events attract large crowds and provide important tourism income for nearby communities. More than 30 years after Dellefors first discovered its potential, the former Dräggängarna quarry remains a striking example of how an industrial site can be given a new purpose.Catch the latest World News and Live updates.
